Tweedie CalculusThanks: I want to thank Alberto Abadie, Isaiah Andrews, and Anna Mikusheva for their guidance.

Santiago Torres ††thanks: Department of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology. 50 Memorial Drive, Cambridge, MA, 02139, USA. storresp@mit.edu
August 24, 2026

Tweedie’s formula is a cornerstone of measurement-error analysis and empirical Bayes. In the Gaussian location model, it recovers posterior means directly from the observed marginal density, bypassing nonparametric deconvolution. Beyond a few classical examples, however, there is no systematic method for determining when such representations exist or how to derive them. This paper develops a general framework for such identities in additive-noise models. I study when posterior functionals admit direct expressions in terms of the observed density—identities I call Tweedie representations—and show that they are characterized by a linear map, the Tweedie functional. Under general conditions, I establish its existence, uniqueness, and continuity. I further show that, in many applications, the Tweedie functional can be expressed as the inverse Fourier transform of an explicit tempered distribution, suitably extended when necessary. This reframes the search for Tweedie-type formulas as a problem in the calculus of tempered distributions. The framework recovers the classical Gaussian case and extends to a broad family of noise distributions for which such representations were previously unavailable. It also goes beyond the standard additive model: in the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model, a change of variables restores the required structure conditionally and yields new Tweedie representations.

1 Introduction

Statistical analysis often seeks to recover latent heterogeneity from noisy measurements. In compound decision, measurement-error, and empirical Bayes problems, objects of interest such as posterior means and decision rules depend on the unknown distribution of latent effects. This naturally shifts attention to recovering that distribution from the data, a task known as deconvolution. Deconvolution, however, is notoriously difficult: it is an ill-posed inverse problem, and the object to be recovered is itself infinite-dimensional.

Tweedie’s formula shows that deconvolution can sometimes be sidestepped altogether. Suppose that Y∼𝒩⁡(X,σ2)Y\sim\mathcal{N}(X,\sigma^{2}), where X∼PXX\sim P_{X} is an unknown latent signal. Robbins (1956) credits Maurice Tweedie with the identity

𝔼⁡[X∣Y=y]=y+σ2​fY′​(y)fY​(y),\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]=y+\sigma^{2}\frac{f_{Y}^{\prime}(y)}{f_{Y}(y)}, (1.1)

where fYf_{Y} is the marginal density of the observable YY. The key feature of this identity is that it represents the posterior mean directly as a function of the observable density, without requiring recovery of the latent distribution PXP_{X}.

Accordingly, Tweedie’s formula opens a different route to estimation and inference: rather than estimating the latent distribution, one may seek to express posterior functionals directly as maps acting on the observed density, which can itself be estimated directly from the data.11 1 In the context of Empirical Bayes, the former approach is known as GG-modeling, the latter as FF-modeling (Efron, 2014; Efron, 2019). This perspective brings several additional benefits. Interpreted as a decision rule, it has a natural shrinkage interpretation: it pulls yy toward regions where the observed data are more likely, with magnitude governed by the score fY′​(y)/fY​(y)f_{Y}^{\prime}(y)/f_{Y}(y). More broadly, such representations entail shape restrictions such as monotonicity (Houwelingen and Stijnen, 1983), and shed light on the statistical difficulty of estimation (Pinkse and Schurter, 2023; Stone, 1983).

A fundamental limitation of this approach is that identities like the Tweedie formula are scattered. Although formulas of this form are available in particular models and for particular estimands, no general framework explains when they exist or how they may be derived.22 2 Most examples have been derived in the case where the observed marginal distribution belongs to an exponential family, since in that case, the posterior distribution can often be written in closed form; see Efron (2011). This paper provides such a framework. I consider general additive-noise models, that is, triplets (Y,X,V)(Y,X,V) of ℝd−\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued random variables related by addition Y=X+VY=X+V. Concretely, I study for a broad class of functions gg and noise distributions VV, when the posterior functional μVg​(y)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)∣Y=y]\mu_{V}^{g}(y)=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y] admits a representation of the form

μVg​(y)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)∣Y=y]=𝒯g,V,y​[fY]fY​(y),\mu_{V}^{g}(y)=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y]=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]}{f_{Y}(y)}, (1.2)

where 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} is a linear functional on a function space containing all possible observed densities, and depending on the estimand gg, the noise law of VV, and the evaluation point yy. I characterize when such functionals exist and how they may be computed in closed form. For instance, in the Gaussian case with g⁡(x)=xg(x)=x, one obtains 𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=y​fY​(y)+σ2​fY′​(y)\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=yf_{Y}(y)+\sigma^{2}f_{Y}^{\prime}(y), which recovers (1.1). I call 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} the Tweedie functional, and any expression of the form (1.2) a Tweedie representation.

The study of these representations naturally leads to three questions that organize the paper:

  1. (i)

    Existence and regularity of the Tweedie functional. Section 3 asks when posterior functionals of the form (1.2) admit a Tweedie functional. I provide sufficient conditions for existence and characterize a natural topology under which this functional is continuous. Theorem 1 establishes existence, uniqueness, and continuity in a broad class of additive-noise models, including settings where (X,V)(X,V) are not independent and where the noise distribution is neither symmetric nor supported on the whole space. Conceptually, the result can be interpreted as an adaptation of the Riesz–Markov theorem to the family of marginal distributions induced by the additive-noise model. At this stage, however, the result is purely existential: it does not yet provide an explicit formula or construction.

  2. (ii)

    Strategy for computing Tweedie representations.

    Section 4 builds on the existence result to develop a general method for deriving Tweedie representations using Fourier analysis. The argument proceeds in two steps. First, Proposition 4.1 shows that the Tweedie functional 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} admits a simple description in frequency coordinates through an associated complex-valued function 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}. The second step is to translate this frequency-side description into an ambient-domain formula acting directly on fYf_{Y}. For this purpose, we notice that under suitable regularity, 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y} in turn defines a linear functional by integration,

    η↦ℐ𝒬g,V,y​[η]≔∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y​(ω)​η​(ω)​𝑑ω.\eta\mapsto\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}[\eta]\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\eta(\omega)\,d\omega.

    This passage from a function to the linear map it induces is standard in the theory of distributions and enlarges the class of objects amenable to Fourier analysis.

    Theorem 2 shows that the relevant mapping is obtained as the inverse Fourier transform of ℐ𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}, or, when necessary, by a suitable extension thereof. This yields a general strategy for computing Tweedie representations in a broad range of settings, since inverse Fourier transforms can often be computed explicitly. The underlying theoretical framework is the theory of tempered distributions, developed by Schwartz (1966) and reviewed in Section 2.

    A major practical advantage of this viewpoint is that it reduces the derivation of Tweedie representations to the computation of inverse Fourier transforms. In this sense, the problem becomes one of calculus. In many cases, the relevant inverse transform can be computed directly or identified from standard transform tables, much as Laplace-transform tables are used in the study of differential equations. Useful references for this purpose include Bateman (1954) and Kammler (2007, Appendix).

  3. (iii)

    Applications. We illustrate the scope of the framework through two applications with new results. First, we use the proposed strategy to derive Tweedie representations for posterior means under a broad family of noise distributions. These examples are summarized in Table 1 at the end of Section 4. To the best of my knowledge, these formulas are new except for the Gaussian and Laplace cases.

    Second, Section 5 studies the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model. This model is widely used for so-called many-means problems, in which researchers make statistical decisions using a large collection of heterogeneous signals, with applications across economics and the social sciences.33 3 Examples include value-added modeling (Chandra et al., 2016; Hull, 2018; Einav et al., 2025), the evaluation of place-based policies (Finkelstein et al., 2021; Chetty and Hendren, 2018), the measurement of discrimination (Kline et al., 2022; Kline et al., 2024; Arnold et al., 2020), policy targeting (Moon, 2025; Yamin, 2025), and research production (Abadie et al., 2026). In this setting, the observation YY is a noisy signal of a latent parameter XX, and the noise covariance matrix Σ\Sigma is allowed to vary across units. The key observation is that the framework developed in this paper applies after conditioning on the realized value of Σ\Sigma. As a result, Tweedie representations of the form (1.2) continue to hold, with the marginal density fYf_{Y} replaced by the conditional density fY|Σ(⋅∣Σ0)f_{Y\mid\Sigma}(\cdot\mid\Sigma_{0}). In this setting, we derive explicit representations not only for posterior means, but also for other posterior functionals that appear in Empirical Bayes analysis.

Relation to the literature.

This paper is most closely related to the literature on Tweedie-type identities in Bayesian, empirical Bayes, and measurement-error problems. Historically, the Gaussian identity appears in print in Dyson (1926), where Dyson attributes it to Arthur Eddington. In a later article, Robbins (1956) reported the formula and credited Maurice Kenneth Tweedie. Much of the subsequent literature develops model-specific analogues or extensions of this identity: West (1982) derives a scale-parameter analogue of Tweedie’s formula for models with known location and unknown scale; Pericchi and Smith (1992) and Pericchi et al. (1993) derive exact relationships for posterior moments and cumulants in normal-location and exponential-family settings; Polson (1991) obtains an exact representation of the posterior mean for location models with normal scale-mixture priors; Robbins (1982) derives a chi-square analogue in the empirical Bayes problem of estimating many variances; Shi and Song (2015) and Shi et al. (2019) develop Laplace-based Tweedie-type formulae and applications to measurement-error and regression problems; and Polson and Sun (2019) give a Gaussian linear-regression version. My contribution differs in emphasis. Rather than deriving a separate identity for each noise model or posterior quantity, I develop a unified framework for establishing the existence of these representations, together with a general strategy for computing them. Within this framework, the classical Gaussian formula, along with many of the extensions studied in the preceding literature, appears as an application of the same underlying argument.

More broadly, this paper relates to the literature on estimating linear functionals in deconvolution problems using Fourier analysis (Fan, 1991; Butucea and Comte, 2009; Pensky, 2017; Hall and Meister, 2007), as well as to other applications of Fourier methods in additive-noise models (Carroll et al., 2006; Meister, 2009; Schennach, 2004a; Schennach, 2004b; Schennach, 2013). In particular, a further consequence of the method is that, in several cases, it yields unbiased estimators of the quantity 𝒯g,V,y​[fY]\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]. This links the framework to the classical literature on unbiased estimation of nonlinear functions of latent variables under additive noise. In the Gaussian case, the problem goes back at least to Kolmogorov (1950), with contemporaneous contributions by Lieberman and Resnikoff (1955) and Healy (1956). A key feature of the present approach is that, once the relevant inverse Fourier transform is identified, it directly delivers explicit functions of the observed variable YY in any finite dimension, and hence unbiased estimators in closed form. In this respect, the method is closely related in spirit to the transform-based constructions of Washio et al. (1956) and Tate (1959), who used other integral transforms to derive formulas for unbiased estimators, and to Ghurye and Olkin (1969), who extended such transform methods to the multivariate setting. Other contributions, notably Stefanski (1989) and Voinov and Nikulin (2012), derive such formulas through power-series expansions of analytic functions. Much of this constructive literature focuses on Gaussian or closely related models. By contrast, the approach developed here is not tied to the Gaussian case and applies to a broader class of noise distributions.

Finally, my results for the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model connect to the nonparametric empirical Bayes literature that allows for dependence between latent effects and the precision with which they are measured. In this setting, the approach developed here provides a route to estimation and inference based directly on the Tweedie representation, without requiring an explicit model for the dependence between the latent parameter and the noise covariance. This contrasts with traditional approaches in the literature, which proceed either through parametric models for the conditional law or through adaptations of nonparametric maximum likelihood methods (Chen, 2022; Weinstein et al., 2018; Kline et al., 2024; George et al., 2017; Chamberlain, 1984; Efron, 2016; Ignatiadis and Wager, 2019; Jiang and Zhang, 2010).

2 Setup and basic notions in Fourier Analysis

This section introduces the additive-noise model studied throughout the paper, states the high-level standing assumptions under which the theory is valid, and records a few immediate consequences. The framework is intentionally broad: it includes the classical Gaussian model underlying Tweedie’s formula, while also accommodating more general deconvolution problems in arbitrary dimensions.

2.1 Setup

Let 𝒫⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) denote the set of probability measures on (ℝd,ℬ⁡(ℝd))(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d})), where ℬ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is the Borel σ\sigma-algebra on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. For a random vector ZZ, I write PZP_{Z} for its law. Consider a triplet of d−d-dimensional random vectors (Y,X,V)(Y,X,V) defined on the same probability space. Here Y∼PYY\sim P_{Y} is the observed vector, X∼PXX\sim P_{X} is the latent signal of interest, and V∼PVV\sim P_{V} is the noise.

For any P∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), let φP:ℝd→ℂ\varphi_{P}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} denote its characteristic function, defined by

φP​(ω)≔∫ℝdei​ω⊤​x​𝑑P​(x)=𝔼Z∼P​[ei​ω⊤​Z],ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{P}(\omega)\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}x}\,dP(x)=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P}\!\left[e^{i\omega^{\top}Z}\right],\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Characteristic functions always exist and uniquely determine the underlying probability law. When Z∼PZZ\sim P_{Z}, I use the shorthand notation φZ≔φPZ\varphi_{Z}\coloneq\varphi_{P_{Z}}.

I now state the main assumptions used throughout the paper.

Assumption 1 (Additivity and Subindependence).

The triplet (Y,X,V)(Y,X,V) is related by addition Y=X+VY=X+V and the characteristic functions satisfy

φY​(ω)=φX​(ω)​φV​(ω),ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{Y}(\omega)=\varphi_{X}(\omega)\varphi_{V}(\omega),\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

As emphasized by Schennach (2019), subindependence is the necessary and sufficient condition for deconvolution. If X⟂⟂VX\perp\!\!\!\!\perp V, then the factorization above holds automatically, but the converse need not be true. Indeed, if φX,V\varphi_{X,V} denotes the joint characteristic function of (X,V)(X,V), then independence requires φX,V​(ω1,ω2)=φX​(ω1)​φV​(ω2)\varphi_{X,V}(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})=\varphi_{X}(\omega_{1})\varphi_{V}(\omega_{2}) for all pairs (ω1,ω2)∈ℝd×ℝd(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, whereas subindependence requires this factorization only on the diagonal ω1=ω2\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}. This weaker condition is appealing because it preserves the convolution structure needed for identification while still allowing possible dependence between the latent signal XX and the noise VV.

Assumption 2 (Identification).

The noise characteristic function is nonzero almost everywhere:

φV​(ω)≠0for Lebesgue-a.e. ​ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{V}(\omega)\neq 0\quad\text{for Lebesgue-a.e. }\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Assumption 2 is the basic nondegeneracy condition behind Fourier deconvolution. Informally, recovering PXP_{X} from the relation φY​(ω)=φX​(ω)​φV​(ω)\varphi_{Y}(\omega)=\varphi_{X}(\omega)\varphi_{V}(\omega) requires division by φV​(ω)\varphi_{V}(\omega). Therefore, this assumption rules out, except on a null set, frequency regions at which inversion breaks down.

Assumption 3 (Noise regularity).

The noise distribution PVP_{V} admits a Lebesgue density fVf_{V}.

Assumption 3 ensures that the observed law PYP_{Y} admits a density. In particular, even if PXP_{X} is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, convolution with a sufficiently regular noise law smooths the distribution of YY enough for it to admit a density.

Proposition 2.1.

Under assumptions 1 and 3, the law PYP_{Y} is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. A version of its density is

fY​(y)=∫ℝdfV​(y−x)​d​PX​(x),y∈ℝd.f_{Y}(y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f_{V}(y-x)\,dP_{X}(x),\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

2.2 Some important notions in Fourier analysis

For 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty and 𝕂∈{ℝ,ℂ}\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}, let Lp​(ℝd,𝕂)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{K}) denote the usual Lebesgue space of measurable 𝕂\mathbb{K}-valued functions on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, identified up to equality almost everywhere, with norm

‖f‖p={(∫ℝd|f⁡(x)|p​dx)1/p,1≤p<∞,ess​supx∈ℝd⁡|f⁡(x)|,p=∞.\|f\|_{p}=\begin{cases}\left(\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|f(x)|^{p}\,dx\right)^{1/p},&1\leq p<\infty,\\[4.30554pt] \operatorname*{ess\,sup}\limits_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}|f(x)|,&p=\infty.\end{cases}

When the codomain is omitted, it is understood to be ℝ\mathbb{R}. Letter ii is reserved for the imaginary unit. z¯\overline{z} denotes the complex conjugate of a number z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}. Let C0​(ℝd,𝕂)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{K}) denote the space of continuous 𝕂\mathbb{K}-valued functions on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that vanish at infinity.

The Fourier transform of a function ψ∈L1​(ℝd,ℂ)\psi\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), denoted by ψ~​(⋅)\widetilde{\psi}(\cdot), is defined as the complex-valued function ψ~:ℝd→ℂ\widetilde{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} given by

ψ~​(ω)≔∫ℝdei​ω⊤​x​ψ​(x)​𝑑x\widetilde{\psi}(\omega)\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}x}\psi(x)dx

Denote by ψ♯\psi^{\sharp} the inverse Fourier transform of ψ\psi, defined as

ψ♯​(x)≔1(2​π)d​∫ℝde−i​ω⊤​x​ψ​(ω)​𝑑ω,x∈ℝd,\psi^{\sharp}(x)\coloneq\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-i\omega^{\top}x}\psi(\omega)\,d\omega,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

whenever the integral is well defined. If, in addition, ψ~∈L1​(ℝd,ℂ)\widetilde{\psi}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), then ψ\psi is Fourier invertible, in that it can be recovered almost everywhere from its Fourier transform through the inversion formula, namely

ψ⁡(x)=ψ~♯​(x)=1(2​π)d​∫ℝde−i​ω⊤​x​ψ~​(ω)​𝑑ω, for Lebesgue - a.e. ​x∈ℝd.\psi(x)=\widetilde{\psi}^{\sharp}(x)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-i\omega^{\top}x}\widetilde{\psi}(\omega)\,d\omega,\quad\text{ for Lebesgue - a.e. }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

This classical L1L^{1} framework is sufficient for many purposes, but it is too restrictive for several objects that arise naturally in analysis and applications. In particular, many functions of interest admit a meaningful Fourier transform even though they do not satisfy the integrability conditions required by the inversion formula above. This motivates the broader framework introduced by Schwartz (1966), now known as the theory of tempered distributions, which places such formal manipulations on a rigorous footing and underlies many successful methods in mathematical physics and applied analysis.

The key construction in this theory is the Schwartz space on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, denoted by 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), consisting of all infinitely differentiable functions whose derivatives of every order decay faster than any inverse polynomial. For instance, it includes all compactly supported C∞−C^{\infty}-functions and the multivariate Gaussian density that decays exponentially fast at infinity. Formally,

𝒮(ℝd)≔{ψ∈C∞(ℝd;ℂ):supx∈ℝd|xα∂βψ(x)|<∞ for all multi-indices α,β∈ℕ0d}.\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\coloneq\left\{\psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}):\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\bigl|x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\psi(x)\bigr|<\infty\text{ for all multi-indices }\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d}\right\}.

where xα≔x1α1⋯xdαdx^{\alpha}\coloneq x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots x_{d}^{\alpha_{d}}, ∂β≔∂|β|/∂x1β1⋯∂xdβd\partial^{\beta}\coloneq\partial^{|\beta|}/\partial x_{1}^{\beta_{1}}\cdots\partial x_{d}^{\beta_{d}}, and |β|=β1+⋯+βd|\beta|=\beta_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{d} are standard multi-index notation.

The Schwartz space is the natural space for Fourier analysis because the map ψ↦ψ~\psi\mapsto\widetilde{\psi} acts particularly well on it: every Schwartz function has a Fourier transform and is Fourier invertible with inverse again in 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Rigorously, the Fourier transform defines a continuous automorphism of 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), mapping the space bijectively and continuously onto itself, with a continuous inverse. This statement is understood relative to the natural topology on 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), induced by the family of seminorms,

pα,β𝒮​(ψ)≔supx∈ℝd|xα​∂βψ⁡(x)|,α,β∈ℕ0d,p^{\mathscr{S}}_{\alpha,\beta}(\psi)\coloneq\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\bigl|x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\psi(x)\bigr|,\quad\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d},

under which 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a Fréchet space.44 4 That is, a complete metrizable locally convex vector space; for a detailed construction of the topology, see Treves (2006, Chapter 10, Example IV).

A tempered distribution on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is a continuous linear functional on 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Thus, the space of tempered distributions corresponds to the topological dual of 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), denoted by 𝒮′​(ℝd)≔(𝒮⁡(ℝd))′\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\coloneq(\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{\prime}. Tempered distributions are also known as generalized functions because they extend the notion of ordinary functions. Indeed, if Q:ℝd→ℂQ:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} is measurable, one may consider the linear map defined by integration,

ψ↦ℐQ​[ψ]=∫ℝdQ⁡(x)​ψ​(x)​𝑑x,ψ∈𝒮⁡(ℝd).\psi\mapsto\mathcal{I}_{Q}[\psi]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Q(x)\psi(x)\,dx,\qquad\psi\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

If this map defines a continuous linear functional on 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), then ℐQ\mathcal{I}_{Q} is a tempered distribution. Common sufficient conditions include QQ being integrable or having at most polynomial growth.55 5 That is, there exist a constant CQ>0C_{Q}>0 and a nonnegative integer NQN_{Q} such that |Q⁡(x)|≤CQ​(1+‖x‖2NQ)|Q(x)|\leq C_{Q}(1+\|x\|_{2}^{N_{Q}}) for almost all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (Strichartz, 2003, pg. 44).

At the same time, 𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) also contains more singular objects. A particularly important example is the point-evaluation map, or Dirac delta, at a∈ℝda\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, denoted by eva\operatorname{ev}_{a}, and defined on Schwartz functions by

eva⁡[ψ]≔ψ⁡(a).\operatorname{ev}_{a}[\psi]\coloneq\psi(a).

Remarkably, the Fourier transform extends naturally from functions to tempered distributions. For T∈𝒮′​(ℝd)T\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the Fourier transform (on tempered distributions), ℱ:𝒮′​(ℝd)→𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{F}:\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), is defined by duality:

ℱ​{T}​[ψ]≔T⁡[ψ~],ψ∈𝒮⁡(ℝd).\mathcal{F}\{T\}[\psi]\coloneq T[\widetilde{\psi}],\quad\psi\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

This is well defined since ψ~∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)\widetilde{\psi}\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) whenever ψ\psi is. By construction, ℱ\mathcal{F} is a continuous automorphism of 𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) under the weak-⋆\star topology: every tempered distribution has a Fourier transform, and every tempered distribution is itself a Fourier transform. The inverse transform is likewise defined by duality,

ℱ−1​{T}​[ψ]≔T⁡[ψ♯].\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{T\}[\psi]\coloneq T[\psi^{\sharp}].

Although both the functional and distributional operators are usually denoted by the same symbol in the literature, I reserve the notation ℱ\mathcal{F} for the operator on 𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and use ψ~\widetilde{\psi} for the ordinary Fourier transform of an integrable function ψ\psi.

3 Existence of the Tweedie functional

This section studies when a linear functional of the latent law PXP_{X} can be represented in terms of the observed density fYf_{Y}. Equivalently, it asks when a feature of the latent distribution can be recovered directly from the marginal density.

For a measurable function ψ:ℝd→ℂ\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}, define

Ψψ​(PX)≔∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​d​PX​(x),\Psi_{\psi}(P_{X})\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,dP_{X}(x),

whenever the integral is well defined. Given a triplet (Y,X,V)(Y,X,V) satisfying Assumptions 1–3, we show that there is a broad class of functions ψ\psi for which one can associate a unique linear functional 𝒯ψ,V\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V} such that Ψψ​(PX)=𝒯ψ,V​[fY]\Psi_{\psi}(P_{X})=\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}[f_{Y}]. Thus, for this class of functionals, the latent quantity of interest admits a representation in terms of the observed density alone. As a corollary, this result implies the existence and uniqueness of the Tweedie functional.

The section also introduces a topology under which the map fY↦𝒯ψ,V​[fY]f_{Y}\mapsto\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}[f_{Y}] is continuous. Although the result established here does not yet provide an explicit expression for 𝒯ψ,V\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}, it lays the foundation for computing Tweedie representations developed in the next section.

Let ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) denote the space of finite signed Radon measures on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. For μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), define its total variation norm by

∥μ∥T​V≔sup{|∫ℝdh(x)dμ(x)|:h∈C0(ℝd),∥h∥∞≤1}.\|\mu\|_{TV}\coloneq\sup\left\{\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}h(x)\,d\mu(x)\right|:h\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\ \|h\|_{\infty}\leq 1\right\}.

It is well known that (ℳ(ℝd),∥⋅∥T​V)\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{TV}\bigr) is a Banach space (Rudin, 1987, Theorem 6.19). Since 𝒫⁡(ℝd)⊆ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subseteq\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the results below apply in particular to probability measures. We nevertheless work on ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) because its vector space structure will be useful throughout.

Given the noise law PVP_{V}, define the convolution operator 𝒦V:ℳ⁡(ℝd)→L1​(ℝd,ℂ)\mathcal{K}_{V}:\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) by

𝒦V​[μ]​(y)≔(fV∗μ)​(y)=∫ℝdfV​(y−x)​𝑑μ​(x),y∈ℝd.\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu](y)\coloneq(f_{V}*\mu)(y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f_{V}(y-x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

The operator 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} is linear and continuous from (ℳ(ℝd),∥⋅∥T​V)\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{TV}\bigr) into (L1(ℝd;ℂ),∥⋅∥1)\bigl(L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}),\|\cdot\|_{1}\bigr), since ‖𝒦V​[μ]‖1≤‖μ‖T​V\|\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]\|_{1}\leq\|\mu\|_{TV}. This operator induces the class of VV-admissible mixtures, denoted as

𝒜V​(ℝd)≔{f=𝒦V​[μ]=fV∗μ:μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)}⊆L1​(ℝd,ℂ).\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\coloneq\{f=\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]=f_{V}*\mu:\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\}\subseteq L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}).

By Proposition 2.1, when the observed density fYf_{Y} exists, it belongs to 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

To characterize 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V}, it is convenient to work in the Fourier domain, building on the extension of characteristic functions introduced above. For μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), define its Fourier–Stieltjes transform by

φμ​(ω)≔∫ℝdei​ω⊤​x​𝑑μ​(x),ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}x}\,d\mu(x),\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Because μ\mu is finite, the integral is well defined for every ω∈ℝd\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. A key fact is the convolution theorem: if f=fV∗μ∈𝒜V​(ℝd)f=f_{V}*\mu\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), then f~​(ω)=φμ​(ω)​φV​(ω)\tilde{f}(\omega)=\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)\varphi_{V}(\omega) for all ω∈ℝd\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The next result uses this identity to show that, under the identification assumption, 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} is invertible on its range.

Proposition 3.1.

Under Assumption 2, the operator 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} is a bijection between ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Proposition 3.1 implies that the inverse 𝒦V−1:𝒜V​(ℝd)→ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{K}_{V}^{-1}:\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is well defined. This makes it natural to equip 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with the pullback of the total variation norm. Specifically, if f∈𝒜V​(ℝd)f\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and f=fV∗μf=f_{V}\ast\mu for some μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), define

‖f‖𝒜V≔‖𝒦V−1​[f]‖T​V=‖μ‖T​V.\|f\|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}}\coloneq\|\mathcal{K}_{V}^{-1}[f]\|_{TV}=\|\mu\|_{TV}.

This definition is unambiguous because the representing measure μ\mu is unique. Furthermore, under this norm, 𝒦V:(ℳ(ℝd),∥⋅∥T​V)→(𝒜V(ℝd),∥⋅∥𝒜V)\mathcal{K}_{V}:\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{TV}\bigr)\to\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}}\bigr) is an isometric isomorphism. It follows that 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) inherits the Banach space structure of ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Having endowed 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with the norm ∥⋅∥𝒜V\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}}, let 𝒜V′​(ℝd)≔(𝒜V​(ℝd))′\mathcal{A}_{V}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\coloneq(\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{\prime} denote its Banach dual, that is, the space of all continuous linear functionals on 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). This is the natural space in which the Tweedie functionals studied in this section will reside.

Theorem 1 (Existence and uniqueness of the representing functional).

Let (Y,X,V)(Y,X,V) satisfy Assumptions 2 and 3. For every ψ∈C0​(ℝd,ℂ)\psi\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), there exists a unique functional 𝒯ψ,V∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

𝒯ψ,V​[𝒦V​[μ]]=∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x)for all ​μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd).\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\!\left[\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,d\mu(x)\qquad\text{for all }\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

In particular, under Assumptions 1, fY=𝒦V​[PX]f_{Y}=\mathcal{K}_{V}[P_{X}], and so

𝒯ψ,V​[fY]=∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​d​PX​(x).\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}[f_{Y}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,dP_{X}(x).

Theorem 1 can be viewed as an adaptation of the Riesz–Markov representation theorem to the class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). The classical Riesz–Markov theorem characterizes continuous linear functionals on C0​(ℝd,ℂ)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) as integration against finite signed regular Borel measures (Conway, 1990, Theorem 5.7). Figure 1 restates this result as a commutative diagram: once the noise law PVP_{V} is fixed, every latent functional Ψψ\Psi_{\psi} factors uniquely through the convolution operator 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} via a continuous linear functional 𝒯ψ,V\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V} on 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). The result is, however, purely existential: it does not yet provide an explicit formula for 𝒯ψ,V\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}.

An immediate corollary of Theorem 1 is the existence and uniqueness of the Tweedie representations under fairly general conditions. By Bayes’ rule, under Assumptions 1 and 3, the posterior functional admits the canonical ratio representation

μVg​(y)=1fY​(y)​[∫ℝdψg,V,y​(x)​d​PX​(x)],ψg,V,y​(x)≔g⁡(x)​fV​(y−x)\mu_{V}^{g}(y)=\dfrac{1}{f_{Y}(y)}\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi_{g,V,y}(x)dP_{X}(x)\right],\quad\psi_{g,V,y}(x)\coloneq g(x)f_{V}(y-x) (3.1)

whenever fY​(y)>0f_{Y}(y)>0. Accordingly, we can formulate the following result.

Corollary 1.1 (Existence and uniqueness of the Tweedie functional).

Fix y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Under assumptions 1, 2, and 3, if ψg,V,y​(x)=g⁡(x)​fV​(y−x)∈C0​(ℝd,ℂ)\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=g(x)f_{V}(y-x)\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), then there exists a unique 𝒯g,V,y∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}\in\mathcal{A}_{V}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that, whenever fY​(y)>0f_{Y}(y)>0,

μVg​(y)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)∣Y=y]=𝒯g,V,y​[fY]fY​(y)\mu_{V}^{g}(y)=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y]=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]}{f_{Y}(y)}
Remark 1.

Assume in addition that fVf_{V} is bounded. Then, for each y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the evaluation map evy:f↦f⁡(y)\operatorname{ev}_{y}:f\mapsto f(y) defines a continuous linear functional on 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Consequently, whenever fY​(y)>0f_{Y}(y)>0, the Tweedie representation can be written as a ratio of continuous linear functionals of fYf_{Y}:

μVg​(y)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)∣Y=y]=𝒯g,V,y​[fY]evy⁡[fY].\mu_{V}^{g}(y)=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y]=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]}{\operatorname{ev}_{y}[f_{Y}]}.

This formulation is useful for inference because it expresses posterior functionals as ratios of linear functionals, a structure that can be exploited to construct valid inferential procedures; see, for example, Ignatiadis and Wager (2022).

Remark 2.

The topology on 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is chosen to obtain the representation results of this section without imposing additional regularity conditions on the latent law. Under stronger assumptions on the mixing distribution—for example, stronger decay of its characteristic function at infinity—one may work with function classes larger than C0​(ℝd,ℂ)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}). This, in turn, enables the representation of a broader class of linear functionals by the same general argument.

4 Computing Tweedie representations

Section 3 established the existence and uniqueness of a linear functional 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} satisfying

μVg​(y)=1fY​(y)​𝒯g,V,y​[fY],𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=∫ℝdψg,V,y​(x)​d​PX​(x),𝒯g,V,y∈𝒜V′​(ℝd).\mu_{V}^{g}(y)=\frac{1}{f_{Y}(y)}\,\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}],\qquad\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi_{g,V,y}(x)\,dP_{X}(x),\qquad\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

That result is, however, too abstract for applications. The goal of this section is to provide a strategy for computing 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} explicitly, via which we can recover the classical Gaussian formula and extend it systematically to more general settings.

The main tool in this endeavor is Fourier analysis. We begin with a standard insight in the deconvolution literature: when ψg,V,y\psi_{g,V,y} is Fourier invertible, the Tweedie functional 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} admits a particularly simple description in frequency coordinates, namely through its action on the characteristic function of the observed variable f~Y=φY\tilde{f}_{Y}=\varphi_{Y}. Proposition 4.1 makes this observation precise. Still, this is not yet the representation we seek: for our purposes, the relevant object must act directly on fYf_{Y}, rather than on its Fourier transforms. The central task of this section is therefore to pass from the frequency-side description furnished by Proposition 4.1 to its ambient-domain counterpart.

The key observation behind this transition is simple: The object identified in Proposition 4.1 is a linear functional evaluated at f~Y\tilde{f}_{Y}, and the natural way to express the same functional as a function of fYf_{Y}, is through the inverse Fourier transform on tempered distributions. Indeed, this is precisely the duality through which the Fourier transform was defined on tempered distributions in Section 2. On its own, however, this argument is only heuristic, since tempered distributions are only defined on the Schwartz class, whereas the densities of interest need not belong to that space. Theorem 2 formalizes the argument and turns it into a general recipe for deriving Tweedie representations: first identify the inverse Fourier image of the Fourier-domain functional on the Schwartz class, where Fourier analysis is canonical; then verify that this object extends continuously to a space large enough to contain the mixture class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). When such an extension exists, it is the desired Tweedie representation. In this way, the problem of finding ambient-domain representations is reduced to the computation of inverse Fourier transforms together with a suitable continuity argument.

The remainder of the section applies this strategy in concrete settings. We begin with cases in which Fourier inversion yields Tweedie representations in the form of expectations of functions of the observed variable. We then turn to posterior mean formulas under specific noise laws, showing how the framework recovers in a few lines the classical Gaussian Tweedie formula and, with equal ease, extends beyond the normal case.

4.1 The Tweedie functional in the Fourier-domain

This subsection shows that, when ψg,V,y\psi_{g,V,y} is Fourier invertible, the map f↦𝒯g,V,y​[f]f\mapsto\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f] admits an explicit representation in the frequency domain. The key ingredient is the Convolution Theorem, according to which the Fourier transform converts convolution in the ambient domain into multiplication in the frequency domain. In particular, if f=fV∗μ∈𝒜V​(ℝd)f=f_{V}\ast\mu\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), then f~​(ω)=φμ​(ω)​φV​(ω)\widetilde{f}(\omega)=\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)\varphi_{V}(\omega), so the mixture structure disentangles and the contribution of the noise can be handled algebraically.

This representation, in turn, condenses the problem into a single complex-valued function, denoted by 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}. The function 𝒬g,V,y​(ω)\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega) is defined almost everywhere by the quotient of ψ~g,V,y​(ω)\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega) and φV​(−ω)\varphi_{V}(-\omega). We call this function the representer of the Tweedie functional in the Fourier domain.

Proposition 4.1 (Fourier-domain representation of the Tweedie functional).

Fix y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Let (Y,X,V)(Y,X,V) satisfy Assumptions 2 and 3. Suppose that

ψg,V,y​(x)≔g⁡(x)​fV​(y−x)∈C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd,ℂ),ψ~g,V,y∈L1​(ℝd,ℂ).\psi_{g,V,y}(x)\coloneq g(x)f_{V}(y-x)\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}),\qquad\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}).

Define

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)≔{ψ~g,V,y​(ω)φV​(−ω),if ​φV​(−ω)≠0,0,if ​φV​(−ω)=0,ω∈ℝd.\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\coloneq\begin{cases}\dfrac{\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)}{\varphi_{V}(-\omega)},&\text{if }\varphi_{V}(-\omega)\neq 0,\\[4.30554pt] 0,&\text{if }\varphi_{V}(-\omega)=0,\end{cases}\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Then the unique functional 𝒯g,V,y∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}\in\mathcal{A}_{V}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) associated with ψg,V,y\psi_{g,V,y} by Theorem 1 admits the representation

𝒯g,V,y​[f]=1(2​π)d​∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y​(ω)​f~​(−ω)​𝑑ω,f∈𝒜V​(ℝd).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f]=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\,\widetilde{f}(-\omega)\,d\omega,\qquad f\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Consequently, if in addition Assumption 1 holds, then the density fYf_{Y} exists and

𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=1(2​π)d​∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y​(ω)​φY​(ω)¯​𝑑ω.\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\,\overline{\varphi_{Y}(\omega)}\,d\omega.

Proposition 4.1 provides an explicit representation of the Tweedie functional in the Fourier domain. Formulas of this type are standard in deconvolution, where they are useful both analytically and statistically; see, for instance, Butucea and Comte (2009) and Pensky (2017). Here, however, their role is different. As discussed above, Proposition 4.1 does not yet deliver the representation of ultimate interest, since the formula still acts in frequency coordinates. Its role is instead to identify the Fourier-side object from which the ambient-domain Tweedie representation will be obtained. The next subsection develops the general argument for carrying out this transition.

4.2 A general strategy for computing Tweedie representations

Proposition 4.1 does more than provide an explicit expression for the Tweedie functional: it also suggests the correct inversion argument. The underlying idea is easiest to state on the Schwartz class. To that end, consider the linear functional induced by the Fourier-domain representer,

ℐ𝒬g,V,y​[ψ]≔∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y​(ω)​ψ​(ω)​𝑑ω.\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}[\psi]\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\psi(\omega)d\omega.

Suppose for the moment that fY∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)f_{Y}\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and that ℐ𝒬g,V,y∈𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Since f~Y​(−ω)=(2​π)d​fY♯​(ω)\widetilde{f}_{Y}(-\omega)=(2\pi)^{d}f_{Y}^{\sharp}(\omega), Proposition 4.1 yields

𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=1(2​π)d​∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y​(ω)​f~Y​(−ω)​𝑑ω=∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y​(ω)​fY♯​(ω)​𝑑ω=ℐ𝒬g,V,y​[fY♯]≕ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}​[fY].\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\,\tilde{f}_{Y}(-\omega)\,d\omega=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)\,f_{Y}^{\sharp}(\omega)\,d\omega=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}[f_{Y}^{\sharp}]\eqqcolon\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}[f_{Y}].

Thus, under sufficient regularity, the Tweedie functional is precisely the inverse Fourier transform of ℐ𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}, understood as a tempered distribution.

If the model class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) were contained in 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and if ℐ𝒬g,V,y∈𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the problem would essentially be solved: one would compute ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} and evaluate the resulting functional at fYf_{Y}. In general, however, the relevant mixture densities need not belong to 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Still, whenever fYf_{Y} does lie in the Schwartz class, Proposition 4.1 forces the representation above. This suggests that, in general, the correct candidate for the Tweedie functional should be obtained as an extension of ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}.

This observation motivates the strategy of the section. We first compute ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} on the Schwartz class, where Fourier inversion is canonical. We then ask whether this object extends continuously to a Banach space EE large enough to contain the relevant mixture densities. If such an extension exists, the density of 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) in EE guarantees uniqueness, and the restriction of that extension to 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is the desired Tweedie functional.

A simple example illustrates the idea. Suppose that 𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=ei​ω⊤​y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=e^{i\omega^{\top}y}. Then, ℐ𝒬g,V,y∈𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and for all ψ∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)\psi\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we obtain

ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}​[ψ]=ℐ𝒬g,V,y​[ψ♯]=∫ℝdei​ω⊤​y​ψ♯​(ω)​𝑑ω=1(2​π)d​∫ℝde−i​ω⊤​y​ψ~​(ω)​𝑑ω=ψ⁡(y),\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}[\psi]=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}[\psi^{\sharp}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}y}\,\psi^{\sharp}(\omega)\,d\omega=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-i\omega^{\top}y}\widetilde{\psi}(\omega)\,d\omega=\psi(y),

where the last equality is the Fourier inversion formula. Hence, ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}=evy\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}=\operatorname{ev}_{y} as tempered distributions.

The key point is that evy\operatorname{ev}_{y} is not confined to the Schwartz class. It makes sense in larger ambient spaces, for instance, C0​(ℝd)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Therefore, if 𝒜V​(ℝd)⊆C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subseteq C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and some other conditions hold, then the extension argument in Theorem 2 will imply that 𝒯g,V,y=evy\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}=\operatorname{ev}_{y} on 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). In that case, the inverse Fourier transform computed on 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) already identifies the correct ambient-domain Tweedie representation. Moreover, we could have used the transform-table identity ℱ−1​{ℐω↦exp⁡(i​ω⊤​y)}=evy\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\omega\mapsto\exp(i\omega^{\top}y)}\}=\operatorname{ev}_{y} to identify the linear maps without any calculations.66 6 For instance, (Kammler, 2007, Appendix A-6).

The next definition isolates the conditions of the ambient space under which this program can be carried out.

Definition 1 (Fourier-compatible ambient space).

Let EE be a Banach space of complex-valued functions on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. For x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define the translation operator (τx​h)​(z)≔h⁡(z−x)(\tau_{x}h)(z)\coloneq h(z-x), z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We say that EE is Fourier-compatible for fVf_{V} if:

  1. (i)(i)

    fV∈Ef_{V}\in E;

  2. (i​i)(ii)

    the inclusion 𝒮⁡(ℝd)↪E\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow E is continuous and has dense range;

  3. (i​i​i)(iii)

    the inclusion E↪L1​(ℝd,ℂ)E\hookrightarrow L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) is continuous;

  4. (i​v)(iv)

    translation is a strongly continuous uniformly bounded group on EE , that is, ME≔supx∈ℝd‖τx‖op<∞M_{E}\coloneq\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\tau_{x}\|_{\text{op}}<\infty, and, for every h∈Eh\in E, ‖τx​h−h‖E→0\|\tau_{x}h-h\|_{E}\to 0 as x→0x\to 0.

The point of Definition 1 is to ensure that the ambient space EE is large enough to contain the entire mixture class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), while still remaining compatible with Fourier analysis. Since every element of 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a convolution fV∗μf_{V}*\mu with a finite measure μ\mu, the key requirement is that EE be stable under averaging translates of fVf_{V}. Conditions (i)–(iv) are imposed precisely for this purpose: they guarantee that fV∈Ef_{V}\in E, that its translates remain in EE with uniform control, and, crucially, that the map x↦τx​fVx\mapsto\tau_{x}f_{V} is continuous in the topology of EE. This continuity ensures that averaging translates of fVf_{V} against a finite measure again produces an element of EE. Consequently, as shown in Lemma A-1, whenever EE is Fourier-compatible for fVf_{V}, then 𝒜V​(ℝd)⊂E\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subset E, which is the basic embedding needed for the extension argument in the main theorem. Finally, the density of 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) in EE guarantees that continuous extensions from the Schwartz class are unique. In particular, once Fourier inversion identifies a candidate for the Tweedie functional on 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), any continuous extension of that map to EE must be unique and therefore coincide with the map we seek.

Theorem 2 (The Tweedie functional as the extension of an inverse Fourier transform).

Fix y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1, and let EE be a Fourier-compatible ambient space for fVf_{V}. Assume there exists N≥0N\geq 0 such that

∫ℝd|𝒬g,V,y​(ω)|(1+‖ω‖)N​𝑑ω<∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{|\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)|}{(1+\|\omega\|)^{N}}\,d\omega<\infty.

Then,

  • a)

    ℐ𝒬g,V,y∈𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and thus ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}∈𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

  • b)

    If, furthermore, ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} extends to a continuous linear functional L𝒬g,V,y∈E′L_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in E^{\prime}, then

    𝒯g,V,y=L𝒬g,V,y|𝒜V​(ℝd).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}=L_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\big|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}.

    Furthermore, since 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is dense in EE, the extension L𝒬g,V,yL_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}} must be unique.

Theorem 2 provides a practical route for computing Tweedie functionals. In short, it shows that the Tweedie functional can be identified via Fourier inversion, provided the resulting map extends continuously to a Fourier-compatible space for the noise density. More importantly, it yields a concrete three-step strategy:

  • •

    Compute the representer of the Tweedie functional in the Fourier domain, 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}.

  • •

    Compute ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} on the Schwartz class 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

  • •

    Verify that this map extends continuously to a larger Fourier-compatible space containing the mixture class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

The remainder of this section illustrates how this strategy can be used to derive Tweedie representations in applications.

4.2.1 Tweedie Representation as an expectation

We examine the case where the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1 hold and 𝒬g,V,y∈L1​(ℝd,ℂ)\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}). In this regime, Theorem 2 is especially easy to apply. As discussed above, the strategy is to first identify ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} on the Schwartz class and then verify that the resulting map extends continuously to an ambient space containing the model class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Indeed, a direct computation shows that, for every η∈𝒮⁡(ℝd)\eta\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}​[η]=∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y♯​(ω)​η​(ω)​𝑑ω⟹ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}=ℐ𝒬g,V,y♯\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}[\eta]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(\omega)\eta(\omega)d\omega\implies\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\}=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}^{\sharp}_{g,V,y}}

The key point is that this formula applies beyond Schwartz regularity: since 𝒬g,V,y♯\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp} is bounded and continuous, the map

f↦∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y♯​(z)​f​(z)​𝑑zf\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(z)f(z)\,dz

is well defined, linear, and continuous on L1​(ℝd,ℂ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}). Moreover, E=L1​(ℝd,ℂ)E=L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) is Fourier-compatible for any noise density fV∈L1​(ℝd)f_{V}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). It follows from Theorem 2 that

𝒯g,V,y​[f]=∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y♯​(z)​f​(z)​𝑑z,f∈𝒜V​(ℝd).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(z)f(z)\,dz,\qquad f\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

We formalize this reasoning in the following result

Proposition 4.2 (Tweedie representation via expectations).

Fix y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1, and define

ψg,V,y​(x)=g⁡(x)​fV​(y−x),𝒬g,V,y​(ω)={ψ~g,V,y​(ω)φV​(−ω),if ​φV​(−ω)≠0,0,if ​φV​(−ω)=0.\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=g(x)f_{V}(y-x),\qquad\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)}{\varphi_{V}(-\omega)},&\text{if }\varphi_{V}(-\omega)\neq 0,\\[4.30554pt] 0,&\text{if }\varphi_{V}(-\omega)=0.\end{cases}

for ω∈ℝd\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Assume further that 𝒬g,V,y∈L1​(ℝd,ℂ)\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}). Then the unique functional 𝒯g,V,y∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}\in\mathcal{A}_{V}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) from Corollary 1.1 satisfies

𝒯g,V,y​[f]=∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y♯​(z)​f​(z)​𝑑z,f∈𝒜V​(ℝd).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(z)\,f(z)\,dz,\qquad f\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Moreover, 𝒬g,V,y♯\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp} is real-valued. If in addition Assumption 1 holds, then fYf_{Y} exists and

𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=∫ℝd𝒬g,V,y♯​(z)​fY​(z)​𝑑z=𝔼⁡[𝒬g,V,y♯​(Y)].\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(z)\,f_{Y}(z)\,dz=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(Y)\right].

Proposition 4.2 shows that, whenever the inverse Fourier image 𝒬g,V,y♯\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp} is sufficiently regular, the Tweedie functional can be represented as an expectation of an explicit function of the observed variable. This is especially useful in practice, since it yields unbiased estimators directly from the observed sample. The following example illustrates this mechanism.

Example - Tweedie functional as an expectation:

Suppose that Y=X+VY=X+V with X⟂⟂VX\perp\!\!\!\!\perp V and V∼𝒩⁡(0,1)V\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). For a>1a>1, consider

g⁡(x)=1a​exp⁡(a2−12​a2​x2).g(x)=\frac{1}{a}\exp\!\left(\frac{a^{2}-1}{2a^{2}}x^{2}\right).

Then, since fV(u)=12​πe−u2/2f_{V}(u)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^{2}/2}, we have

ψg,V,y​(x)=e(a2−1)​y22​12​π​a​exp⁡(−(x−a2​y)22​a2),ψ~g,V,y​(ω)=exp⁡((a2−1)​y22+i​ω​a2​y−a2​ω22).\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=e^{\frac{(a^{2}-1)y^{2}}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,a}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-a^{2}y)^{2}}{2a^{2}}\right),\quad\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\exp\!\left(\frac{(a^{2}-1)y^{2}}{2}+i\omega a^{2}y-\frac{a^{2}\omega^{2}}{2}\right).

Hence, since φV(ω)=e−ω2/2\varphi_{V}(\omega)=e^{-\omega^{2}/2},

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=ψ~g,V,y​(ω)φV​(−ω)=exp⁡((a2−1)​y22+i​ω​a2​y−(a2−1)​ω22).\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\frac{\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)}{\varphi_{V}(-\omega)}=\exp\!\left(\frac{(a^{2}-1)y^{2}}{2}+i\omega a^{2}y-\frac{(a^{2}-1)\omega^{2}}{2}\right).

Proposition 4.2 then yields

𝒯g,V,y[fY]=𝔼[𝒬g,V,y♯(Y)],𝒬g,V,y♯(z)=e(a2−1)​y2212​π​(a2−1)exp(−(z−a2​y)22​(a2−1)).\boxed{\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(Y)\right],\quad\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(z)=e^{\frac{(a^{2}-1)y^{2}}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(a^{2}-1)}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-a^{2}y)^{2}}{2(a^{2}-1)}\right).}

In particular, given an i.i.d. random sample Y1,…,YnY_{1},\dots,Y_{n}, we can produce an unbiased estimator

𝔼⁡[1n​∑i=1n𝒬g,V,y♯​(Yi)]=𝔼⁡[𝒬g,V,y♯​(Y)]=𝒯g,V,y​[fY].\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(Y_{i})\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}^{\sharp}(Y)\right]=\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}].

4.3 Tweedie representations in smooth models

We now turn to the case in which the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1 hold, but the symbol 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y} is no longer integrable and instead has at most polynomial growth. In this regime, ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} is typically expressed in terms of derivatives of the argument, so the relevant ambient space must encode smoothness. For this reason, L1​(ℝd,ℂ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) is no longer an appropriate extension space. A natural alternative is provided by spaces of smooth functions vanishing at infinity. For k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, define

C0k​(ℝd,ℂ)≔{ψ∈Ck​(ℝd,ℂ):∂αψ∈C0​(ℝd,ℂ)​ for all ​|α|≤k},C_{0}^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C})\coloneq\left\{\psi\in C^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}):\partial^{\alpha}\psi\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C})\text{ for all }|\alpha|\leq k\right\},

and consider the normed space

Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)≔C0k​(ℝd,ℂ)∩L1​(ℝd,ℂ),‖ψ‖Ξk≔max|α|≤k⁡‖∂αψ‖∞+‖ψ‖1.\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C})\coloneq C_{0}^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}),\qquad\|\psi\|_{\Xi^{k}}\coloneq\max_{|\alpha|\leq k}\|\partial^{\alpha}\psi\|_{\infty}+\|\psi\|_{1}.
Assumption 4 (Noise smoothness of order kk).

For some k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, the noise density fVf_{V} belongs to C0k​(ℝd,ℝ)C_{0}^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}).

Assumption 4 suggests that a natural ambient space in this setting is Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), since one expects mixtures generated by fVf_{V} to inherit the same degree of smoothness as the noise kernel. The next lemma makes this precise by showing both that the mixture class 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is contained in Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) and that Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) is Fourier-compatible for fVf_{V}. This framework covers many common noise laws whose densities are smooth and vanish at infinity, including Gaussian, logistic, Gumbel, Laplace, and Cauchy distributions, among others.

Lemma 1 (The space Ξk\Xi^{k} is Fourier-compatible).

Assume Assumption 4 with smoothness order kk. Then 𝒜V​(ℝd)⊂Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subset\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) and Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) is Fourier-compatible for fVf_{V}.

We now apply the strategy of Theorem 2 to identify cases in which the Tweedie functional 𝒯g,V,y\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y} admits representations as a finite linear combination of weighted derivatives of the density.

Proposition 4.3 (Tweedie representation via factorization of measures.).

Fix y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1, and also Assumption 4 with order k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. Suppose there exists a family of finite signed Radon measures {μα:|α|≤k}⊂ℳ⁡(ℝd)\{\mu_{\alpha}:|\alpha|\leq k\}\subset\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=∑|α|≤k(i​ω)α​φμα​(ω)for Lebesgue-a.e. ​ω∈ℝd,\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}(i\omega)^{\alpha}\varphi_{\mu_{\alpha}}(\omega)\qquad\text{for Lebesgue-a.e. }\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

where φμα\varphi_{\mu_{\alpha}} is the Fourier-Stieltjes transform of μα\mu_{\alpha}. Then 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y} has at most polynomial growth, hence ℐ𝒬g,V,y∈𝒮′​(ℝd)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Moreover, the map

Lg,V,y​[ψ]≔∑|α|≤k∫ℝd∂αψ⁡(z)​d​μα​(z),ψ∈Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ),L_{g,V,y}[\psi]\coloneq\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\partial^{\alpha}\psi(z)\,d\mu_{\alpha}(z),\qquad\psi\in\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}),

defines a continuous linear functional on Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), and is the unique continuous extension of ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} from 𝒮⁡(ℝd)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) to Ξk​(ℝd,ℂ)\Xi^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}). Hence, the unique functional 𝒯g,V,y∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}\in\mathcal{A}_{V}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) from Corollary 1.1 satisfies

𝒯g,V,y=Lg,V,y|𝒜V​(ℝd).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}=L_{g,V,y}\big|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}.

If in addition Assumption 1 holds, then fYf_{Y} exists and

𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=Lg,V,y​[fY]=∑|α|≤k∫ℝd∂αfY​(z)​d​μα​(z).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=L_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\partial^{\alpha}f_{Y}(z)\,d\mu_{\alpha}(z).

Proposition 4.3 treats the case in which the Fourier-domain representer 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y} can be written as a polynomial in ω\omega, with coefficients given by Fourier transforms of a finite collection of measures. In that case, the Tweedie functional admits a representation as a finite linear combination of weighted derivatives of fYf_{Y}. In the special case k=0k=0, this reduces to integration against a finite measure. Furthermore, if μ0\mu_{0} is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, the resulting formula becomes the expectation of the density of μ0\mu_{0} evaluated at YY, and therefore delivers a closed-form unbiased estimator. We now use this result to recover the classical Tweedie formula.

Example - Original Tweedie’s formula:

Suppose d=1d=1, Y=X+VY=X+V, X⟂⟂VX\perp\!\!\!\!\perp V, and V∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)V\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}). Let g⁡(x)=xg(x)=x. Since the Gaussian density is C0∞​(ℝ)C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), the smoothness assumption holds for every kk. A direct calculation gives

ψg,V,y(x)=xfV(y−x),ψ~g,V,y(ω)=(y+iσ2ω)ei​ω​ye−σ2ω2/2.\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=xf_{V}(y-x),\qquad\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\bigl(y+i\sigma^{2}\omega\bigr)e^{i\omega y}e^{-\sigma^{2}\omega^{2}/2}.

Since φV(−ω)=e−σ2ω2/2\varphi_{V}(-\omega)=e^{-\sigma^{2}\omega^{2}/2}, it follows that

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=ψ~g,V,y​(ω)φV​(−ω)=(y+i​σ2​ω)​ei​ω​y.\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\frac{\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)}{\varphi_{V}(-\omega)}=\bigl(y+i\sigma^{2}\omega\bigr)e^{i\omega y}.

Now ei​ω​y=φδy​(ω)e^{i\omega y}=\varphi_{\delta_{y}}(\omega), so

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=y​φδy​(ω)+(i​ω)​φσ2​δy​(ω).\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=y\,\varphi_{\delta_{y}}(\omega)+(i\omega)\,\varphi_{\sigma^{2}\delta_{y}}(\omega).

Hence Proposition 4.3 applies with k=1k=1,

μ0=y​δy,μ1=σ2​δy.\mu_{0}=y\,\delta_{y},\qquad\mu_{1}=\sigma^{2}\delta_{y}.

Therefore,

𝒯g,V,y​[fY]=∫ℝfY​(z)​d​μ0​(z)+∫ℝfY′​(z)​d​μ1​(z)=y​fY​(y)+σ2​fY′​(y).\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{Y}(z)\,d\mu_{0}(z)+\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{Y}^{\prime}(z)\,d\mu_{1}(z)=yf_{Y}(y)+\sigma^{2}f_{Y}^{\prime}(y).

Dividing by fY​(y)f_{Y}(y), we recover the classical Tweedie formula:

𝔼⁡[X∣Y=y]=𝒯g,V,y​[fY]fY​(y)=y+σ2​fY′​(y)fY​(y).\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]}{f_{Y}(y)}=y+\sigma^{2}\frac{f_{Y}^{\prime}(y)}{f_{Y}(y)}.}

We now turn to a non-Gaussian example, showing that the same method applies just as naturally under Laplace noise.

Example - Posterior mean under Laplace noise:

Suppose d=1d=1, Y=X+VY=X+V, X⟂⟂VX\perp\!\!\!\!\perp V, and VV has Laplace noise:

fV(u)=12​be−|u|/b,b>0.f_{V}(u)=\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|u|/b},\qquad b>0.

Let g⁡(x)=xg(x)=x. Since fV∈C0​(ℝ)f_{V}\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}), the smoothness assumption holds with k=0k=0. In this setting

ψg,V,y​(x)=x​fV​(y−x),ψ~g,V,y​(ω)=ei​ω​y​(y1+b2​ω2+2​i​b2​ω(1+b2​ω2)2).\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=xf_{V}(y-x),\qquad\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=e^{i\omega y}\left(\frac{y}{1+b^{2}\omega^{2}}+\frac{2ib^{2}\omega}{(1+b^{2}\omega^{2})^{2}}\right).

Since φV​(−ω)=11+b2​ω2\varphi_{V}(-\omega)=\frac{1}{1+b^{2}\omega^{2}}, it follows that

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=ψ~g,V,y​(ω)φV​(−ω)={(y+2​i​b2​ω1+b2​ω2)​ei​ω​y if ω≠±i/b,0 otherwise.\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=\frac{\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)}{\varphi_{V}(-\omega)}=\begin{cases}\left(y+\frac{2ib^{2}\omega}{1+b^{2}\omega^{2}}\right)e^{i\omega y}&\text{ if }\omega\neq\pm i/b,\\ 0&\text{ otherwise}.\\ \end{cases}

Now ei​ω​y=φδy​(ω)e^{i\omega y}=\varphi_{\delta_{y}}(\omega). Also, let νy\nu_{y} be the measure with Lebesgue density dνy(z)≔sgn(z−y)e−|z−y|/bdzd\nu_{y}(z)\coloneq\text{sgn}(z-y)e^{-|z-y|/b}\,dz. Then, a direct calculation shows that

φνy​(ω)=2​i​b2​ω1+b2​ω2​ei​ω​y⟹𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=y​φδy​(ω)+φνy​(ω)ω​ a.e.\varphi_{\nu_{y}}(\omega)=\frac{2ib^{2}\omega}{1+b^{2}\omega^{2}}e^{i\omega y}\implies\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=y\,\varphi_{\delta_{y}}(\omega)+\varphi_{\nu_{y}}(\omega)\quad\omega\text{ a.e.}

Therefore Proposition 4.3 applies with k=0k=0 and μ0=y​δy+νy\mu_{0}=y\delta_{y}+\nu_{y}, yielding

𝒯g,V,y[fY]=∫ℝfY(z)dμy(z)=yfY(y)+∫ℝsgn(z−y)e−|z−y|/bfY(z)dz.\mathcal{T}_{g,V,y}[f_{Y}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{Y}(z)\,d\mu_{y}(z)=yf_{Y}(y)+\int_{\mathbb{R}}\text{sgn}(z-y)e^{-|z-y|/b}f_{Y}(z)\,dz.

Dividing by fY​(y)f_{Y}(y), we obtain

𝔼[X∣Y=y]=y+1fY​(y)[∫ℝsgn(z−y)e−|z−y|/bfY(z)dz]\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]=y+\dfrac{1}{f_{Y}(y)}\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}}\text{sgn}(z-y)e^{-|z-y|/b}f_{Y}(z)\,dz\right]}

As with the original Tweedie formula, the representation under Laplace noise still admits a shrinkage interpretation. Unlike the Gaussian case, however, the adjustment is not driven by derivatives of the density. Instead, the shrinkage rule is non-local: it depends on values of the density away from the point yy, rather than only on local slope information.

Proposition 4.3 describes only one family of Tweedie representations for the smooth models. Other useful families are developed in Appendix B using the same general techniques. More broadly, even when a case falls outside these families, the computation of Tweedie functionals can often still be carried out on a case-by-case basis by applying the general strategy developed in this section.

We conclude this section by illustrating the flexibility of the method across a range of noise distributions. Table 1 reports posterior mean representations for several noise laws, with the corresponding derivations collected in Appendix B.2. One noteworthy conclusion that emerges from these examples is that the local structure of the original Tweedie formula appears to be a distinctive feature of the Gaussian case.

5 Tweedie representations in the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model

We now derive Tweedie representations for several empirical Bayes estimands in the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model in arbitrary dimension. Although this model is widely used in practice, it falls outside the framework studied in the previous sections because the noise covariance is itself random. I will show, however, that this complication is not insurmountable. The key observation is that, conditional on a realization of Σ\Sigma, the model can be rescaled to the standard Gaussian sequence form analyzed above. The general theory therefore applies conditional on Σ\Sigma and can be used to derive Tweedie functionals acting on the conditional density without any further assumption on the problem.

Let 𝕊+⁣+d\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d} denote the set of symmetric positive definite d×dd\times d matrices. The model we consider is

Y=X+Σ1/2​V,Y=X+\Sigma^{1/2}V,

where V∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)V\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), (X,Σ)∼PX,Σ(X,\Sigma)\sim P_{X,\Sigma}, and (X,Σ)⟂⟂V(X,\Sigma)\perp\!\!\!\!\perp V.

This model is standard in empirical Bayes applications in economics and related social sciences. A common interpretation is that YY is an estimator of a latent parameter XX, constructed from a sample mean or, more generally, from an asymptotically linear statistic. A central limit theorem then justifies a Gaussian approximation to the estimation error. Heteroskedasticity arises naturally when sample sizes, sampling designs, or underlying population variability differ across analysis units, so that the covariance matrix of the estimator is itself unit-specific. It is therefore natural to treat (X,Σ)(X,\Sigma) as drawn from a joint superpopulation distribution PX,ΣP_{X,\Sigma}. This formulation allows, in particular, for dependence between the latent parameter and the noise level. It is common practice to consider Σ\Sigma to be known and equal to a sample-based estimate.

For a measurable function g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, our objects of interest are conditional expectations of the form

𝔼[g(X)∣Y=y,Σ=Σ0].\mathbb{E}\!\left[g(X)\mid Y=y,\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}\right].

If the distribution of Σ\Sigma were degenerate at Σ0∈𝕊+⁣+d\Sigma_{0}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}, this would be the usual posterior quantity 𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)∣Y=y]\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y] under Gaussian noise with covariance matrix Σ0\Sigma_{0}. The difficulty here is that Σ\Sigma is random, so the model is not, at the outset, of the additive form studied in the previous sections. This difficulty disappears once we condition on Σ=Σ0\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}. To see this, define

Z≔Σ0−1/2Y,W≔Σ0−1/2X,z0≔Σ0−1/2y.Z\coloneq\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}Y,\qquad W\coloneq\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}X,\qquad z_{0}\coloneq\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}y.

Then, conditional on Σ=Σ0\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}, we have Z=W+VZ=W+V, W⟂⟂VW\perp\!\!\!\!\perp V, V∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)V\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). In particular,

φZ|Σ​(ω∣Σ0)=φW|Σ​(ω∣Σ0)​φV​(ω),\varphi_{Z\mid\Sigma}(\omega\mid\Sigma_{0})=\varphi_{W\mid\Sigma}(\omega\mid\Sigma_{0})\varphi_{V}(\omega),

so, conditional on Σ=Σ0\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}, the standardized model satisfies the same structural conditions as the additive Gaussian model studied in Sections 3 and 4. The existence and Fourier representation results developed there therefore apply conditional on Σ\Sigma, and hence pointwise in Σ0\Sigma_{0}. The next corollary records this implication formally.

Corollary 2.1 (Conditional existence and representation of the Tweedie functional in the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model).

Fix a version of the regular conditional law PX|ΣP_{X\mid\Sigma}. For PΣP_{\Sigma}-almost every Σ0∈𝕊+⁣+d\Sigma_{0}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}, define W≔Σ0−1/2XW\coloneq\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}X, Z≔Σ0−1/2YZ\coloneq\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}Y, z0≔Σ0−1/2yz_{0}\coloneq\Sigma_{0}^{-1/2}y. Let g:ℝd→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable.

  • a)

    If the expectations below are well defined, then fZ|Σ​(z0∣Σ0)>0f_{Z\mid\Sigma}(z_{0}\mid\Sigma_{0})>0 and

    𝔼[g(X)∣Y=y,Σ=Σ0]=∫ℝdg⁡(Σ01/2​w)​ϕ​(z0−w)​d​PW|Σ​(w∣Σ0)fZ|Σ​(z0∣Σ0).\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y,\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}]=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}g(\Sigma_{0}^{1/2}w)\,\phi(z_{0}-w)\,dP_{W\mid\Sigma}(w\mid\Sigma_{0})}{f_{Z\mid\Sigma}(z_{0}\mid\Sigma_{0})}.
  • b)

    Let ψg,y,Σ0​(w)≔g⁡(Σ01/2​w)​ϕ​(z0−w)\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}(w)\coloneq g(\Sigma_{0}^{1/2}w)\,\phi(z_{0}-w). If ψg,y,Σ0∈C0​(ℝd,ℂ)\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), then there exists a unique continuous linear functional 𝒯ψg,y,Σ0,V∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}},V}\in\mathcal{A}_{V}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

    𝒯g,y,Σ0[fZ|Σ(⋅∣Σ0)]=∫ℝdψg,y,Σ0(w)dPW|Σ(w∣Σ0).\mathcal{T}_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}\!\left[f_{Z\mid\Sigma}(\cdot\mid\Sigma_{0})\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}(w)\,dP_{W\mid\Sigma}(w\mid\Sigma_{0}).

    Consequently,

    𝔼[g(X)∣Y=y,Σ=Σ0]=𝒯ψg,y,Σ0,V[fZ|Σ(⋅∣Σ0)]fZ|Σ​(z0∣Σ0).\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mid Y=y,\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}]=\frac{\mathcal{T}_{\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}},V}\!\left[f_{Z\mid\Sigma}(\cdot\mid\Sigma_{0})\right]}{f_{Z\mid\Sigma}(z_{0}\mid\Sigma_{0})}.
  • c)

    If, in addition, ψg,y,Σ0∈Ξ0​(ℝd,ℝ)\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}\in\Xi^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}) and Fourier invertible, define

    𝒬g,y,Σ0​(ω)≔ψ~g,y,Σ0​(ω)φV​(−ω),ω∈ℝd.\mathcal{Q}_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}(\omega)\coloneq\frac{\widetilde{\psi}_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}(\omega)}{\varphi_{V}(-\omega)},\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

    Then,

    ∫ℝdψg,y,Σ0​(w)​d​PW|Σ​(w∣Σ0)=1(2​π)d​∫ℝd𝒬g,y,Σ0​(ω)​φZ|Σ​(ω∣Σ0)¯​𝑑ω.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}(w)\,dP_{W\mid\Sigma}(w\mid\Sigma_{0})=\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{Q}_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}(\omega)\overline{\varphi_{Z\mid\Sigma}(\omega\mid\Sigma_{0})}d\omega.

The corollary implies that, once we condition on Σ=Σ0\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}, the heteroskedastic problem can be handled with the same computational strategy developed in Section 4. In particular, Tweedie formulas can be obtained by working with the Fourier-domain representer 𝒬g,y,Σ0\mathcal{Q}_{g,y,\Sigma_{0}}, exactly as in the additive Gaussian model after the appropriate standardization. We next apply this approach to a range of empirical Bayes estimands. In contrast to Table 1, which centers on posterior means, the discussion here also covers other posterior features. Additional derivations used in these examples are gathered in Appendix C.

6 Conclusion

Tweedie’s formula shows that, in some settings, features of the posterior distribution can be recovered directly from the observed marginal density, without solving a nonparametric deconvolution problem. This paper develops a general framework for such identities in additive-noise models. The main contribution is twofold. First, I characterize when posterior functionals admit a representation of this form through a linear map acting on the observed density—the Tweedie functional—and establish existence, uniqueness, and continuity under general conditions. Second, I provide a constructive method for deriving such representations by Fourier analysis, showing that the relevant operator can be obtained from the inverse Fourier transform of an explicitly characterized tempered distribution, or from a suitable extension thereof.

This perspective turns the search for Tweedie-type formulas into a tractable problem in the calculus of tempered distributions. In particular, it recovers the classical Gaussian identity, yields new representations for posterior means under a broad family of noise laws, and in some cases also delivers unbiased estimators directly from the observed data. The framework therefore provides a unified route to evaluation of posterior functionals that avoids explicit recovery of the latent distribution and is not tied to exponential-family structure or to Gaussian noise.

The paper also shows that the method is not confined to the standard additive model. In the heteroskedastic Gaussian sequence model, conditioning on the realized covariance matrix and applying an appropriate change of variables restores the structure needed for the theory to apply. This yields new Tweedie representations for posterior means and other empirical Bayes functionals, without imposing additional structure on the model. More broadly, the results suggest that many estimation problems built on this model, which are typically approached through deconvolution together with additional restrictions to restore tractability, may instead be studied through direct representations of posterior quantities in terms of the observable conditional density.
