A.1 Proof of Proposition 2.1

Proof.

Recall that for any Borel set AA, the convolution measure PX∗PVP_{X}\ast P_{V} is defined as

(PX∗PV)(A)=∬ℝd×ℝd𝟙{x+v∈A}dPX(x)dPV(v)(P_{X}\ast P_{V})(A)=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbbm{1}\{x+v\in A\}dP_{X}(x)dP_{V}(v)

Its characteristic function is

φPX∗PV​(ω)\displaystyle\varphi_{P_{X}\ast P_{V}}(\omega) =∫ℝdei​ω⊤​y​d​(PX∗PV)​(y)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}y}\,d(P_{X}\ast P_{V})(y)
=∬ℝd×ℝdei​ω⊤​(x+v)​d​PX​(x)​d​PV​(v)\displaystyle=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}(x+v)}\,dP_{X}(x)\,dP_{V}(v)
=(∫ℝdei​ω⊤​x​d​PX​(x))​(∫ℝdei​ω⊤​v​d​PV​(v))\displaystyle=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}x}\,dP_{X}(x)\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}v}\,dP_{V}(v)\right)
=φX​(ω)​φV​(ω).\displaystyle=\varphi_{X}(\omega)\varphi_{V}(\omega).

By Assumption 1,

φY​(ω)=φX​(ω)​φV​(ω)=φPX∗PV​(ω)for all ​ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{Y}(\omega)=\varphi_{X}(\omega)\varphi_{V}(\omega)=\varphi_{P_{X}\ast P_{V}}(\omega)\qquad\text{for all }\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Since characteristic functions uniquely determine probability laws, it follows that PY=μ=PX∗PV.P_{Y}=\mu=P_{X}*P_{V}.

Now let A∈ℬ⁡(ℝd)A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Since PVP_{V} admits the density fVf_{V}, Tonelli’s theorem allows

PY​(A)\displaystyle P_{Y}(A) =(PX∗PV)​(A)\displaystyle=(P_{X}*P_{V})(A)
=∬ℝd×ℝd𝟙{x+v∈A}fV(v)dvdPX(x)\displaystyle=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbbm{1}\{x+v\in A\}\,f_{V}(v)\,dv\,dP_{X}(x)
=∫ℝd(∫ℝd𝟙A​(x+v)​fV​(v)​𝑑v)​d​PX​(x).\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbbm{1}_{A}(x+v)f_{V}(v)\,dv\right)dP_{X}(x).

For each fixed xx, the change of variables y=x+vy=x+v gives

∫ℝd𝟙A​(x+v)​fV​(v)​𝑑v=∫AfV​(y−x)​𝑑y.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbbm{1}_{A}(x+v)f_{V}(v)\,dv=\int_{A}f_{V}(y-x)\,dy.

Hence, by Tonelli’s theorem again,

PY​(A)\displaystyle P_{Y}(A) =∫ℝd(∫AfV​(y−x)​𝑑y)​d​PX​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\int_{A}f_{V}(y-x)\,dy\right)dP_{X}(x)
=∫A(∫ℝdfV​(y−x)​d​PX​(x))​𝑑y.\displaystyle=\int_{A}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f_{V}(y-x)\,dP_{X}(x)\right)dy.

Therefore, PYP_{Y} is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, with density

fY​(y)=∫ℝdfV​(y−x)​d​PX​(x)f_{Y}(y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f_{V}(y-x)\,dP_{X}(x)

for Lebesgue-a.e. yy. ∎

A.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1

Proof.

Surjectivity is immediate from the definition of 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), since

𝒜V​(ℝd)=𝒦V​(ℳ⁡(ℝd)).\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\mathcal{K}_{V}\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr).

It therefore remains to prove injectivity. Since 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} is linear, it is enough to show that its kernel is trivial. Let μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfy

𝒦V​[μ]=fV∗μ=0in ​L1​(ℝd,ℂ).\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]=f_{V}*\mu=0\qquad\text{in }L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}).

Write

φμ​(ω)≔∫ℝdei​ω⊤​x​𝑑μ​(x),ω∈ℝd,\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\omega^{\top}x}\,d\mu(x),\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

for the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of μ\mu. Since μ\mu is finite, φμ\varphi_{\mu} is bounded and continuous, with

|φμ​(ω)|≤‖μ‖T​Vfor all ​ω∈ℝd.|\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)|\leq\|\mu\|_{TV}\qquad\text{for all }\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Taking Fourier transforms gives

𝒦V​[μ]~​(ω)=(fV∗μ)~​(ω)=f~V​(ω)​φμ​(ω)=φV​(ω)​φμ​(ω),ω∈ℝd,\widetilde{\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]}(\omega)=\widetilde{(f_{V}*\mu)}(\omega)=\widetilde{f}_{V}(\omega)\,\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)=\varphi_{V}(\omega)\varphi_{\mu}(\omega),\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

where we used that f~V=φV\widetilde{f}_{V}=\varphi_{V} because fVf_{V} is the density of PVP_{V}. Since 𝒦V​[μ]=0\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]=0 in L1​(ℝd,ℂ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), its Fourier transform vanishes identically, and hence

φV​(ω)​φμ​(ω)=0for all ​ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{V}(\omega)\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)=0\qquad\text{for all }\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Now let

D≔{ω∈ℝd:φV​(ω)≠0}.D\coloneq\{\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\varphi_{V}(\omega)\neq 0\}.

By Assumption 2, the complement of DD has Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, DD is dense in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Therefore

φμ​(ω)=0for all ​ω∈D.\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)=0\qquad\text{for all }\omega\in D.

Since φμ\varphi_{\mu} is continuous and vanishes on a dense set, it follows that

φμ​(ω)=0for all ​ω∈ℝd.\varphi_{\mu}(\omega)=0\qquad\text{for all }\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

By the uniqueness theorem for Fourier–Stieltjes transforms, this implies μ=0\mu=0. Hence ker⁡(𝒦V)={0}\ker(\mathcal{K}_{V})=\{0\}, so 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} is injective. ∎

A.3 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

Define

Iψ:ℳ⁡(ℝd)→ℝ,Iψ​[μ]≔∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x).I_{\psi}:\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathbb{R},\qquad I_{\psi}[\mu]\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,d\mu(x).

Since ψ∈C0​(ℝd,ℂ)\psi\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}), the map IψI_{\psi} is linear and continuous with respect to the total variation norm. Indeed,

|Iψ​[μ]|≤‖ψ‖∞​‖μ‖T​V,μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd).|I_{\psi}[\mu]|\leq\|\psi\|_{\infty}\,\|\mu\|_{TV},\qquad\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

By Proposition 3.1, the operator

𝒦V:(ℳ(ℝd),∥⋅∥T​V)→(𝒜V(ℝd),∥⋅∥𝒜V)\mathcal{K}_{V}:\bigl(\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{TV}\bigr)\to\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}}\bigr)

is an isometric isomorphism. We may therefore define

𝒯ψ,V≔Iψ∘𝒦V−1.\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\coloneq I_{\psi}\circ\mathcal{K}_{V}^{-1}.

This map is linear. Moreover, if f∈𝒜V​(ℝd)f\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and μ=𝒦V−1​[f]\mu=\mathcal{K}_{V}^{-1}[f], then

|𝒯ψ,V​[f]|=|Iψ​[μ]|≤‖ψ‖∞​‖μ‖T​V=‖ψ‖∞​‖f‖𝒜V.|\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}[f]|=|I_{\psi}[\mu]|\leq\|\psi\|_{\infty}\,\|\mu\|_{TV}=\|\psi\|_{\infty}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal{A}_{V}}.

Hence 𝒯ψ,V∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Now let μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Then

𝒯ψ,V​[𝒦V​[μ]]=Iψ​[μ]=∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x),\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\!\left[\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]\right]=I_{\psi}[\mu]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,d\mu(x),

which proves the claimed representation.

Finally, under Assumptions 1 and 3, Proposition 2.1 implies that

fY=fV∗PX=𝒦V​[PX].f_{Y}=f_{V}*P_{X}=\mathcal{K}_{V}[P_{X}].

Therefore, taking μ=PX\mu=P_{X} in the previous display gives

𝒯ψ,V​[fY]=𝒯ψ,V​[𝒦V​[PX]]=∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​d​PX​(x)=Ψψ​(PX).\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}[f_{Y}]=\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\!\left[\mathcal{K}_{V}[P_{X}]\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,dP_{X}(x)=\Psi_{\psi}(P_{X}).

To prove uniqueness, let S∈𝒜V′​(ℝd)S\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) also satisfy

S⁡[𝒦V​[μ]]=∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x)for all ​μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd).S\!\left[\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,d\mu(x)\qquad\text{for all }\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Since 𝒦V\mathcal{K}_{V} is surjective onto 𝒜V​(ℝd)\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), every f∈𝒜V​(ℝd)f\in\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) can be written as f=𝒦V​[μ]f=\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu] for some μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Hence

S⁡[f]=S⁡[𝒦V​[μ]]=∫ℝdψ⁡(x)​𝑑μ​(x)=𝒯ψ,V​[𝒦V​[μ]]=𝒯ψ,V​[f].S[f]=S\!\left[\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi(x)\,d\mu(x)=\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}\!\left[\mathcal{K}_{V}[\mu]\right]=\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}[f].

Thus S=𝒯ψ,VS=\mathcal{T}_{\psi,V}.
∎

A.4 Proof of Theorem 2

We begin with a technical lemma:

Lemma A-1 (Bochner convolution in a Fourier-compatible ambient space).

Let EE satisfy items (3)(3)–(4)(4) of Definition 1. Then, for every h∈Eh\in E and every μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the map

x⟼τx​hx\longmapsto\tau_{x}h

is continuous from ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} into EE, satisfies

‖τx​h‖E≤ME​‖h‖E(x∈ℝd),\|\tau_{x}h\|_{E}\leq M_{E}\|h\|_{E}\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}),

and belongs to L1​(|μ|,E)L^{1}(|\mu|;E). Define

h∗Eμ≔∫ℝdτx​h​𝑑μ​(x)∈E.h*_{E}\mu\coloneq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\tau_{x}h\,d\mu(x)\in E.

Then

‖h∗Eμ‖E≤ME​‖h‖E​‖μ‖T​V.\|h*_{E}\mu\|_{E}\leq M_{E}\|h\|_{E}\|\mu\|_{TV}.

Moreover, if J:E↪L1​(ℝd,ℂ)J:E\hookrightarrow L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) denotes the continuous inclusion, then

J⁡(h∗Eμ)=J⁡(h)∗μin ​L1​(ℝd,ℂ),J(h*_{E}\mu)=J(h)*\mu\qquad\text{in }L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}),

where the right-hand side is the usual convolution. In particular, if fV∈Ef_{V}\in E, then

𝒜V​(ℝd)={fV∗μ:μ∈ℳ⁡(ℝd)}⊂E.\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\{f_{V}*\mu:\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\}\subset E.

The same conclusion holds for absolutely continuous measures d​μ​(x)=η⁡(x)​d​xd\mu(x)=\eta(x)\,dx with η∈L1​(ℝd)\eta\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):

∫ℝdη⁡(x)​τx​h​𝑑x∈EandJ⁡(∫ℝdη⁡(x)​τx​h​𝑑x)=J⁡(h)∗η.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\eta(x)\tau_{x}h\,dx\in E\quad\text{and}\quad J\!\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\eta(x)\tau_{x}h\,dx\right)=J(h)*\eta.
Proof.

Since (τx)x∈ℝd(\tau_{x})_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}} is strongly continuous, the map fh:ℝd→Ef_{h}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to E, fh​(x)≔τx​hf_{h}(x)\coloneq\tau_{x}h is continuous. Because ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is separable, its image fh​(ℝd)f_{h}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a separable subset of EE; hence fhf_{h} is strongly measurable. Moreover, ‖fh​(x)‖E=‖τx​h‖E≤ME​‖h‖E\|f_{h}(x)\|_{E}=\|\tau_{x}h\|_{E}\leq M_{E}\|h\|_{E} for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Because J:E→L1​(ℝd,ℂ)J:E\to L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}) is continuous and linear, it commutes with Bochner integration (Hsing and Eubank, 2015, Theorem 3.1.7 ). Therefore

To identify this with the usual convolution, note that for J⁡(h)∈L1J(h)\in L^{1},

This proves

The absolutely continuous case follows by taking d​μ​(x)=η⁡(x)​d​xd\mu(x)=\eta(x)\,dx, with η∈L1​(ℝd)\eta\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). The inclusion 𝒜V​(ℝd)⊂E\mathcal{A}_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subset E follows by applying the result to h=fV∈Eh=f_{V}\in E.

Appendix B Derivation of posterior means for various noise laws

This appendix records the Fourier calculations underlying the entries in Table 1. Throughout, we specialize to the posterior mean case g⁡(x)=xg(x)=x in dimension d=1d=1, so that

ψg,V,y​(x)=x​fV​(y−x).\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=x\,f_{V}(y-x).

The general strategy is the same in every example: first compute the symbol 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y} from Proposition 4.1, then identify the inverse Fourier transform ℱ−1​{ℐ𝒬g,V,y}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\} using the machinery developed in Section 4.

B.1 Auxiliary results

The next lemma isolates the common calculation that is used repeatedly below.

Lemma B-1 (Universal formula for the posterior mean in dimension one).

Assume d=1d=1, g⁡(x)=xg(x)=x, and fix y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}. Let ψg,V,y​(x)=x​fV​(y−x)\psi_{g,V,y}(x)=x\,f_{V}(y-x), and suppose that ψg,V,y∈L1​(ℝ,ℂ)\psi_{g,V,y}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{C}) and ψ~g,V,y∈L1​(ℝ,ℂ)\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{C}). ψ~g,V,y​(ω)=ei​ω​y​[y​φV​(−ω)−i​dd​ω​φV​(−ω)],ω∈ℝ,\widetilde{\psi}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=e^{i\omega y}\left[y\,\varphi_{V}(-\omega)-i\frac{d}{d\omega}\varphi_{V}(-\omega)\right],\qquad\omega\in\mathbb{R},

=ei​ω​y​[y​∫ℝe−i​ω​u​fV​(u)​𝑑u−∫ℝu​e−i​ω​u​fV​(u)​𝑑u].\displaystyle=e^{i\omega y}\left[y\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-i\omega u}f_{V}(u)\,du-\int_{\mathbb{R}}u\,e^{-i\omega u}f_{V}(u)\,du\right].

dd​ω​φV​(−ω)=∫ℝ(−i​u)​e−i​ω​u​fV​(u)​𝑑u,\frac{d}{d\omega}\varphi_{V}(-\omega)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}(-iu)e^{-i\omega u}f_{V}(u)\,du,

The Hilbert transform is a fundamental tool in signal processing and in the study of singular integral operators in harmonic analysis. It also appears in Tweedie representations since it is the inverse transform of the tempered distribution induced by the map ω↦−i​sgn​(ω)\omega\mapsto-i\text{sgn}(\omega).

Proposition B.1 (Tweedie representation via the Hilbert-transform).

Assume d=1d=1. Fix y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R} and let g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1, and also Assumption 4 with order k=1k=1. Suppose there exist cg,V,y∈ℂc_{g,V,y}\in\mathbb{C} and a measurable function kg,V,y:(0,∞)→ℂk_{g,V,y}:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{C} such that

∫01t​|kg,V,y​(t)|​𝑑t<∞,∫1∞|kg,V,y​(t)|​𝑑t<∞,\int_{0}^{1}t\,|k_{g,V,y}(t)|\,dt<\infty,\qquad\int_{1}^{\infty}|k_{g,V,y}(t)|\,dt<\infty,

and

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=ei​ω​y​(−i​π​cg,V,y​sgn⁡(ω)+∫0∞(e−i​ω​t−ei​ω​t)​kg,V,y​(t)​𝑑t)\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=e^{i\omega y}\left(-i\pi c_{g,V,y}\,\operatorname{sgn}(\omega)+\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigl(e^{-i\omega t}-e^{i\omega t}\bigr)k_{g,V,y}(t)\,dt\right)

for Lebesgue-a.e. ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R}. Then 𝒬g,V,y\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y} has at most linear growth, hence ℐ𝒬g,V,y∈𝒮′​(ℝ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}}\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}). Moreover, the map

Lg,V,y​[ψ]≔π​cg,V,y​ℋ​[ψ]​(y)+∫0∞(ψ⁡(y−t)−ψ⁡(y+t))​kg,V,y​(t)​𝑑t,ψ∈Ξ1​(ℝ,ℂ),L_{g,V,y}[\psi]\coloneq\pi c_{g,V,y}\,\mathcal{H}[\psi](y)+\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigl(\psi(y-t)-\psi(y+t)\bigr)k_{g,V,y}(t)\,dt,\qquad\psi\in\Xi^{1}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{C}),

The following family will also be needed to compute some of the examples:

Proposition B.2 (Tweedie representation via one-sided compensated kernels).

Assume d=1d=1. Fix y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R} and let g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be measurable. Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1, and also Assumption 4 with order k=1k=1. If in addition Assumption 1 holds, then

B.2 Computation of table entries

Posterior mean for Normal⁡(μ,σ2)\mathrm{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^{2}).

By Lemma B-1,

𝒬g,V,y​(ω)=ei​ω​y​[y−μ+i​σ2​ω]=(y−μ)​φδy​(ω)+(i​ω)​φσ2​δy​(ω).\mathcal{Q}_{g,V,y}(\omega)=e^{i\omega y}\left[y-\mu+i\sigma^{2}\omega\right]=(y-\mu)\,\varphi_{\delta_{y}}(\omega)+(i\omega)\,\varphi_{\sigma^{2}\delta_{y}}(\omega).

Follows from example above with λ=1\lambda=1:

𝔼[X∣Y=y]=y−μ+1fY​(y)[∫ℝsgn(z−y)e−|z−y|/bfY(z)dz].\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]=y-\mu+\frac{1}{f_{Y}(y)}\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}}\operatorname{sgn}(z-y)e^{-|z-y|/b}f_{Y}(z)\,dz\right].}

Since

Since
